basic_info.name: Refik Anadol
basic_info.location: Los Angeles, California, USA (born Istanbul, Turkey, 1985)

practice_description.medium: Data sculpture, generative AI installation, architectural projection, real-time generative video
practice_description.practice_summary: Refik Anadol creates large-scale data sculptures and immersive installations that use machine learning to process vast datasets — museum archives, nature recordings, urban data, neurological signals — transforming them into continuously evolving visual environments that reveal latent patterns invisible to human perception.
practice_description.methodology: Anadol and his studio (RAS, ~team of multidisciplinary artists, architects, data scientists) train custom AI models using frameworks like NVIDIA StyleGAN2 ADA on massive datasets. They developed a proprietary Latent Space Browser (since 2017) to navigate high-dimensional embedding spaces and select outputs. Works often incorporate site-specific environmental inputs (light, sound, weather, movement) that modulate the generative output in real-time. The process typically involves: (1) ethically sourcing or partnering with institutions for large datasets, (2) training custom models on those datasets, (3) exploring the latent space for aesthetic possibilities, (4) creating real-time rendering systems that respond to environmental conditions. Recent work with the Large Nature Model involves training on 500+ million data points from nature.

relevance_to_sense_room.relevance_summary: Anadol's practice of transforming institutional archives and ecological datasets into living generative environments is directly relevant to A(DAI)'s concept of art as primary material in a graph-curated exhibition. His work demonstrates how machine learning can reveal hidden relationships within large collections — a computational analog to graph-based curation.
relevance_to_sense_room.art_as_substrate: Yes. Anadol's data sculptures function as continuously generating visual substrates. Unsupervised at MoMA transformed 200 years of art history into a living, breathing visual field that served as both artwork and ambient environment. The outputs are designed to be immersive grounds rather than discrete objects.
relevance_to_sense_room.relational_composition: Partially. The internal logic of the ML models discovers relationships between data points (images, sounds, ecological records) and renders them as visual continuities. However, the relational structure is latent within the model rather than explicitly graph-based. The connections are discovered by the algorithm rather than curated through explicit relational composition.
relevance_to_sense_room.self_recomposing: Yes. Works continuously generate new visual states. Unsupervised incorporated real-time environmental data (light, movement, acoustics, weather) from MoMA's lobby to modulate output. The Large Nature Model generates endlessly evolving nature visualizations. No frame is ever repeated.

works.title: Unsupervised — Machine Hallucinations — MoMA
works.description: Processed 138,151 images from MoMA's entire collection through StyleGAN2, displayed as a continuously evolving data sculpture in the museum's Gund Lobby. Over 3 million visitors; average viewing time 38 minutes. Acquired by MoMA as the first generative artwork in its permanent collection. Environmental data from the lobby modulated output in real-time.
works.relevance: Demonstrates how an institutional collection can become substrate for a living generative artwork. The model discovers latent relationships between 200 years of art — a machine-learning parallel to graph-based curation of artistic connections.

works.title: Large Nature Model (LNM)
works.description: The world's first open-source generative AI model dedicated to nature, trained on 500+ million ethically sourced data points from the Smithsonian, National Geographic, Natural History Museum London, and field recordings from 16 rainforest locations. Multimodal (images, audio, video, text). Debuted at World Economic Forum Davos 2024.
works.relevance: Directly relevant as infrastructure: an open-source, ethically sourced AI model that generates from nature data. The commons orientation of the model (open-source, institutional partnerships, ethical data collection) aligns with A(DAI)'s commons-first values. Shows how art practice can produce open infrastructure.

works.title: WDCH Dreams
works.description: Projected ML-processed visualizations of 100 years of the LA Philharmonic's digital archives onto Frank Gehry's Walt Disney Concert Hall. Architecture as screen, institutional memory as generative material.
works.relevance: Demonstrates building-as-canvas and institutional archive-as-material — the architectural environment becomes a generative system driven by cultural data.

protocol_art_resonance.protocol_art_summary: Anadol's practice increasingly treats the construction of AI models and data pipelines as creative acts. The Large Nature Model is simultaneously an artwork, a research tool, and open infrastructure — the model itself is the artistic output as much as any visual rendering. Dataland (his planned AI museum) represents institution-building as creative practice.
protocol_art_resonance.system_designed: The Large Nature Model (LNM) — an open-source multimodal generative AI model for nature. The Latent Space Browser — a proprietary tool for navigating high-dimensional embedding spaces. Dataland — a museum and Web3 platform dedicated to AI art, opening Spring 2026 in Los Angeles in a Gehry-designed building.

commons_orientation.commons_summary: The Large Nature Model is explicitly open-source, built on Meta's open-source Llama models, and trained on ethically sourced institutional data. Anadol has publicly advocated for the importance of open-source AI. However, the studio's commercial practice (gallery sales, commissioned installations, NFT releases through platforms like Feral File) operates within proprietary art market structures. Dataland is a private museum initiative. The practice is hybrid: commons-oriented infrastructure (LNM) alongside commercial art production.

governance_model.governance_detail: Refik Anadol Studio (RAS) is led by Anadol as primary creative director, co-founded with Efsun Erkilic who handles operational leadership. The studio employs a multidisciplinary team but creative direction flows from Anadol. Partnerships with institutions (Smithsonian, Google, NVIDIA, Meta) shape data access and compute resources but not artistic decisions.

consent_and_authorship.consent_approach: Data is sourced through institutional partnerships (Smithsonian, Natural History Museum, MoMA) with explicit permission. For the Large Nature Model, Anadol emphasizes 'ethically harnessed' open-source data. Field recordings from rainforests are self-collected by the studio. No personal data from individuals is used as primary material (the MoMA work uses artwork metadata, not visitor data).
consent_and_authorship.authorship_model: Solo authorship credited to Refik Anadol, with studio acknowledged as RAS. Machine co-authorship is implicit — the AI models generate the visual output — but Anadol frames this as 'machine hallucination' rather than machine co-creation. The artist retains full authorial credit.

liveness_and_duration.temporal_detail: Installations render in real-time, continuously generating new visual states. Unsupervised incorporated live environmental data (light, sound, weather, movement) to modulate output. The Large Nature Model can generate indefinitely from its training. Works are designed to never repeat — each moment is unique. Duration in exhibition contexts ranges from months (Unsupervised ran almost a year at MoMA) to permanent installation.

data_materiality.data_sources: Museum collection metadata and images (MoMA's 138,151 works), nature imagery and audio (500M+ data points from Smithsonian, National Geographic, Natural History Museum London, 16 rainforest field recordings), architectural archives (LA Philharmonic's 100-year digital archive), EEG neurological data (Melting Memories), urban data, satellite imagery, coral reef images (135 million for Serpentine show).
data_materiality.data_provenance: Institutional partnerships with explicit permission for MoMA, Smithsonian, Natural History Museum, National Geographic. Self-collected field data from rainforests using LiDAR, photogrammetry, and audio capture. Public domain and openly licensed datasets. Anadol emphasizes ethical sourcing as a core value. The LNM is described as using 'the most extensive, ethically collected dataset of the natural world.'

embedding_space_relevance.embedding_summary: Central to the practice. Anadol's work is fundamentally about navigating and rendering latent/embedding spaces. The studio's custom Latent Space Browser (developed since 2017) allows exploration of 1,024-dimensional embedding spaces created by StyleGAN2 models. The 'machine hallucination' aesthetic is the visual manifestation of traversing these high-dimensional spaces. The Large Nature Model creates multimodal embeddings across image, audio, video, and text.
embedding_space_relevance.multimodal: Yes. The Large Nature Model is explicitly multimodal — trained on and capable of generating across text, images, audio, and video in a unified framework. Earlier works were primarily visual, but the practice is expanding toward full multimodal synthesis.

exhibition_modality.spatial_description: Works manifest as large-scale LED screens (Unsupervised: 24' x 24'), architectural projections (WDCH Dreams projected onto Gehry's building), and immersive room-scale installations. Dataland will be a 20,000 sq ft purpose-built museum. The scale is consistently architectural — the work occupies and transforms the space it inhabits rather than sitting within it as an object.

interoperability.composability: The Large Nature Model, as an open-source AI model, is inherently composable — its outputs can serve as inputs for other systems. The model itself can be fine-tuned or extended. However, individual installation works are self-contained and do not expose APIs or produce outputs designed for external consumption.
interoperability.technical_openness: Hybrid. The Large Nature Model is open-source (built on Meta's Llama). The Latent Space Browser and studio's proprietary tools are closed. Individual installations are closed systems. The practice straddles open infrastructure (LNM) and closed artistic production.

technical_approach.stack: NVIDIA StyleGAN2 ADA for generative models, Meta Llama for Large Nature Model foundation, custom Latent Space Browser for high-dimensional navigation, Google Cloud for sustainable compute, NVIDIA GPUs for training and inference, LiDAR and photogrammetry for field data collection, large-scale LED display technology, real-time rendering systems with environmental sensor integration.

network_position.scene_affiliation: AI art, data art, new media art, immersive/experiential art. Strong connections to both the commercial art world (major gallery representation, MoMA acquisition) and the technology industry (Google, NVIDIA, Meta partnerships). Bridges art world, tech industry, and institutional/museum contexts. Also connected to the Web3/NFT art ecosystem through Feral File and other platforms.
network_position.connections: teamLab (shared territory of large-scale immersive installations attracting mass audiences, though different technical approaches). Vladan Joler (both engage with AI infrastructure as artistic subject, but from opposite positions — Anadol celebrates ML aesthetics while Joler critically maps its extractive costs). Ian Cheng (both use real-time generative systems, but Cheng's are simulation-based while Anadol's are ML-based).

potential_role_in_adai.role_detail: Anadol's work demonstrates how large datasets can become living generative substrates — directly relevant to A(DAI)'s graph-based intelligence becoming exhibition material. The Large Nature Model's open-source, ethically-sourced approach offers a model for commons-oriented AI art infrastructure. However, the studio's scale, commercial positioning, and individual-genius framing may not align with A(DAI)'s collective, commons-first ethos. Most useful as a reference for: (1) how latent space navigation can reveal hidden connections in collections, (2) how open-source AI models can be artistic outputs, (3) how institutional data partnerships work in practice.
